newsitem.title: USA: Few respond to Miami truck money amnesty.
newsitem.headline: Few respond to Miami truck money amnesty.

text.p: A 48-hour "amnesty" that allowed Miami residents to return thousands of dollars that disappeared after a security truck crash ended on Saturday, leaving police holding only about $20 of returned funds.
Police officials also said that two women, including a Dade County corrections employee, were arrested on Friday for allegedly trying to use food stamps from the truck crash site.

Police declared the "no questions asked" amnesty on Thursday -- one day after a Brink's armoured security truck believed to be carrying $3.7 million flipped on a highway overpass, cracked open and sent a waterfall of bundled currency and coins into the impoverished neighbourhood below.

Residents of the neighbourhood, one of Miami's poorest, and passing motorists seized the opportunity to gather the cash, some filling bags with coins, others scrambling on their hands and knees to snare the windfall. Many said they viewed the accident as a gift from God, who sent "pennies from heaven."
Afterward, estimates were that some $500,000 or more had disappeared, most of it nearly impossible to trace.

The task of recovering the stolen money prompted police to give the city 48 hours to return the funds without facing theft charges. But the amnesty came and went at mid-day on Saturday, and police said only two people had come forward.
"Only one woman has come in," a police spokesman said.

On Friday, Faye McFadden, a single mother of six, returned $19.53 in quarters and pennies that she had gathered in a shopping bag. McFadden, 40, said she wanted to set a good example for her children.
And Herbert Tarvin, an 11-year-old, gave the 85-cents he had picked up to his teachers after he heard them talking about the accident.

The two women who were arrested. Marcia Scott, a pretrial services technician with the corrections department, and Phyllis King, whose occupation was not released, had $8,000 worth of food stamps believed to be from the Brink's truck in their possession when they were picked up on a tip at a Miami supermarket on Friday, police said.
The incident has led to some soul searching in Miami, a city with a high violent crime rate that is reeling under the effects of a municipal government scandal and $68 million budget deficit.

Newspaper columnists and talk radio callers have weighed in on the issue, some decrying the dishonesty of those who had gathered the money, others defending the hopelessness faced by the inner city residents photographed scooping up coins.

The Miami Herald on Friday asked its readers how they would respond if a wrecked Brink's truck left $10,000 on their street. On Saturday, the paper said more than 1,000 responded, most falling into two categories: 517 said they would turn in the money because it was the right thing to do, and 446 said they would keep it and feel no guilt.
